cells.tense: You are tending what is shared and it is holding, right now.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Name what's finished in a shared practice you tend and what isn't, then skip the finished part for a week and see what stands.
cells.core:
There's something you're tending that belongs to more than you — a practice, a way people meet, a story that gets retold. You give it steady, patient attention, and it's answering. It can hold some weight without your hands on it. You can watch something you've grown carry on and not step in to steady it. That's the whole look of this going well: care that doesn't grip.

The part that's finished is the part hardest to leave alone. Release what's done; keep tending what isn't. What you've already given it taught you what it needs. In a shared thing, stopping is what lets it stand by itself. The next time you'd adjust something already steady, wait and see what happens.
cells.sheetLine: What you tend can hold some weight without you.
cells.verb: Tending what is shared until it can carry itself
cells.place: Inside a shared thing passed down and still held

cells.tense: You will have gripped the shared thing before it has a chance to grow.
cells.act: explore the feeling with fresh sensitivity
cells.ask: Before you fix or improve one shared thing, sit with how it actually feels right now — let yourself notice it before you touch it.
cells.core:
A shared thing sits with you and you're already at the next version of it — what it will be when it's better, when it's shaped right. Your hands get in before it has a life. You're tending it so hard it can't breathe, and the people in it watch you not let it stay still.

Something of yours is being skipped: the feeling of what's here now, before you improve it. Sit with one shared thing and notice what it is, not what it should be. Then you can decide what to touch. Reaching ahead isn't the problem — what hurts is not letting anything catch up to you. Let one thing be as it is for a week.

cells.tense: You were part of something shared and you have not come back to it.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Pick a modest thing you'd want to carry forward — a question, a practice, a way of meeting people — and start it because it interests you, no destination attached.
cells.core:
You were part of something shared and you haven't been in it since. The door closed behind you and you're still at it. What you knew how to tend is still yours, but it isn't in your hands, and the days go by with nothing of it growing.

Start one thing of your own — not a duty, not a re-entry, just something you want to see. The spark of starting is its own fuel. You don't need the old thing to let you back in. Take a direction with no destination yet and follow it for a week. See what it asks of you.

cells.tense: You are carrying a shared thing forward and calling it nobody's doing.
cells.act: bear the duty and know when to let go
cells.ask: Next time you'd quietly keep a shared practice alive, just notice your part in it — that noticing alone is the whole act, nothing has to follow.
cells.core:
A shared thing stays alive because somebody keeps it on the calendar, remembers the words, shows up first. Ask and you'd say it's just how things are done here, that anyone would. Doing it well looks like knowing the weight is yours, then choosing it again. The effort runs without your say-so, so it tires you more than it should.

Before you take it up again, feel the weight as something you're choosing — that's the whole change. Then carry it or don't, with your eyes open. The duty itself was fine. Doing it while saying it isn't you is what wears you down. Once you own it, you can set it down when it's finished.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that this person is the one carrying a particular shared thing — the record says tending happens through shared meaning, not that a specific tradition is theirs alone to transmit. A reader could reasonably say the sharing is mutual, that others carry it too, and my cell would still give them something usable because noticing what you're actually holding is worth doing whether or not you're the only one holding it. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'what you tend can hold weight without you' — it's prettier than it is true of any single person's week. Watch the noun-making: 'the letting go,' 'the reaching,' 'the keeping' all smuggled a verb into a thing. Watch scope: 'never' and 'always' overreach the card's claim about one capacity. Watch the library refrains — 'on its own,' 'in front of you,' 'still standing,' 'you're the one,' 'one small thing — and keep the sheet lines to a single beat each.
